transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi... yeah, thank you for seeing me. So, um, I guess I'm here because things have just gotten really, really overwhelming lately, and honestly not in a way I expected at all? 

I mean, I’ve always done art—just, you know, for myself, mostly—and my friends and family always said, "Oh, you should sell this, you should do commissions," and I finally decided to take the plunge and actually try to turn it into a real freelance business. I have my associate's degree, so I figured I could figure out the business side, right? I thought it would be great, setting my own hours, doing what I love. 

But ever since I actually started trying to do it, it's like... it's just this constant, heavy weight. I keep getting so incredibly wound up over the administrative side of things. Like sending invoices, or even just looking at client messages. An email notification will pop up on my phone and my stomach just drops to the floor. And instead of just opening it and dealing with it, I... I just avoid them. I’ll put my phone in a completely different room, or I'll go organize a drawer in the kitchen that doesn't even need organizing, and I'll just avoid the messages for days. 

It builds up so much in my head that I just end up sitting there, completely paralyzed, crying at my kitchen table over an email about a watercolor commission. It’s ridiculous. And the worst part is that it’s bleeding into everything else in my life, too. Because I'm so wrapped up in avoiding the freelance stuff and stressing over it, I'm completely forgetting normal, everyday stuff. Like, I completely forgot to pay my electric bill last month because my brain was just so fried from worrying about an invoice I hadn't sent. I just... I don't know why I can't just handle it, but it's really getting out of hand.
Has this kind of avoidance—putting things off or feeling overwhelmed by everyday tasks—happened in other parts of your life before, or is this mostly just with your freelance work?

No, honestly, it's really just the freelance stuff. Like, I've never been someone who just ignores things until they become a problem, you know? I mean, sure, I might procrastinate on doing the dishes for a night if I'm tired, or put off doing laundry until the weekend, but that's just normal stuff. It's never been like this, where I'm actively hiding from my responsibilities. 

In fact, I've always been pretty organized. Even when I was getting my associate's degree, I had a whole system. I had this color-coded planner, and I would map out all my assignments and exams weeks in advance. I never missed a deadline, and I never felt this... this paralyzing dread about doing the work. I would just sit down at my desk, open my laptop, and do it. It was straightforward. And even with my art before, when I was just doing it for fun, I could spend hours painting or sketching and it felt relaxing. It felt like an escape. 

But now, it's like the moment money or clients are involved, my brain just short-circuits. It's so frustrating because I know I'm capable of handling things. I managed a whole household when I was in school, I kept on top of everything, but now... now just the thought of opening my email app makes my heart race. I just don't understand why this one specific thing—this thing that was supposed to be a dream come true—is causing me to act so completely out of character. I've never avoided life like this before. Never.

When you feel that dread or fear about opening an email or dealing with client messages, do you also notice any physical reactions, like your heart racing, sweating, shaking, or feeling short of breath?

Well, I mean... no, not really like that. I mean, I did say my heart races, and it does, definitely, it beats a little faster when I see the notification pop up, but it's not like I'm having a full-blown panic attack, you know? I don't get all sweaty or start shaking or anything dramatic like that. I'm definitely not gasping for air. 

It's more just this... this awful, heavy sinking feeling in my stomach, like I mentioned before. Like when you realize you forgot something really important, but that feeling just stays there. And I get this tension right in my shoulders and the back of my neck. I'll realize I've been sitting there staring at the phone with my shoulders practically up to my ears, just totally clenched up. And sometimes I'll get a little bit of a headache if I let myself stress about it for too long, which I usually do, honestly. 

But no, it's not like I'm trembling or dripping with sweat. It's just this intense, overwhelming mental block that makes me want to run in the opposite direction. Like, I'll literally walk out of the room just to get away from the phone. I remember last Tuesday, I got a message from a client asking for a revision on a sketch, which is totally normal, right? Revisions are part of the process. But I saw the preview on my lock screen, and my chest just tightened up, and instead of opening it, I went and scrubbed the bathtub. I spent forty-five minutes scrubbing a tub that was already clean just so I didn't have to look at it. So, it's that kind of physical reaction—just tension and this desperate urge to escape—but not the shaking or shortness of breath.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or afraid specifically in situations where your work or performance might be judged or evaluated by others?

Well, I don't think it's about being judged, exactly? I mean, art is subjective, right? So someone is always going to have an opinion on it, and I've been sharing my art online for years. I have an Instagram account where I post my sketches and watercolors, and I've had people leave comments saying they don't like my style or that I messed up the proportions on a hand or something. And honestly, that never really bothered me. I'd just brush it off or even agree with them sometimes, because, you know, hands are incredibly hard to draw. So it's not like I'm terrified of someone looking at my work and saying, "Oh, this isn't very good." 

And even back when I was in school, getting my associate's, we had to do these presentations where we'd stand up in front of the whole class and talk about our projects, and the professor would critique us right there on the spot. I never loved doing it—I don't think anyone really enjoys public speaking—but I never had this kind of reaction to it. I'd just get up, do my presentation, take the feedback, and sit back down. It was fine. 

But with this freelance stuff, it feels different. It's not about them judging the art itself, I don't think. It's more about... the business transaction part of it? Like, the expectation that I have to deliver something perfect because they're paying me for it, and the fear that I'm going to mess up the invoice, or miss a deadline, or say the wrong thing in an email and look unprofessional. It's the administrative, professional side of it that feels so heavy. Like, if a client asks for a revision, my brain doesn't go, "Oh, they hate my art, they're judging me." My brain goes, "Oh my god, I have to figure out how to respond to this email professionally, and adjust the timeline, and what if I charge them wrong for the extra time, and what if they get mad because I took too long to reply?" 

So, yeah, it's not really a fear of being evaluated on my performance or my skills, if that makes sense. It's just the overwhelming pressure of all the strings attached to it now that it's a business. It just feels like there are so many ways to fail that have nothing to do with actually painting.
Outside of the freelance work stress, do you find yourself feeling persistently worried or on edge about other things in your life, like everyday responsibilities or events?

No, not really. Honestly, the rest of my life is pretty calm right now. I mean, my husband works full-time, and we have our routine, you know? He goes to work, I take care of the house, I run the errands, I make sure the bills are paid on time. And none of that bothers me at all. Like, going to the grocery store, figuring out what to make for dinner, making sure the car gets its oil changed—I'm totally fine with all of that. I actually kind of like it. I've always liked having a routine and keeping things organized, like I mentioned before with my planner in college. 

I'm not sitting around worrying about, I don't know, whether the roof is going to leak or if we're going to get in a car accident or something. I don't lay awake at night stressing about my health or my family's health. My parents live a few towns over, and we see them every other weekend, and everything is fine there. We have a couple of friends we see for game nights sometimes, and I never worry about those things either. I don't get anxious about hosting or what people think of the appetizers I made. 

It's really just this one specific thing. If you took the freelance business completely out of the equation, I'd say I'm probably one of the least stressed people you'd meet. I've always been pretty even-keeled. Even when we were buying our house a few years ago, which everyone says is the most stressful thing you can do, I was fine. I just made a checklist, gathered all the documents the bank needed, and checked things off one by one. I didn't lose any sleep over it. So, yeah, it's definitely not a general, everyday kind of worry. It's just... it's just this business. Everything else is completely normal and manageable.
Have you been feeling down, sad, or hopeless for most of the day, more days than not, even when you're not thinking about the freelance work?

No, not at all. I really don't feel sad or hopeless. I mean, if I'm not thinking about the freelance stuff, I'm actually a pretty upbeat person. Like I was saying about my routine earlier, I genuinely enjoy my day-to-day life. When I wake up, if I know I don't have to check that specific work email account, I feel completely fine. I'll make my coffee, maybe sit out on the patio for a bit if the weather's nice—lately it's been a little chilly in the mornings, but I still like to just sit and watch the birds for a few minutes before I start my chores around the house. And during all that, I feel perfectly content. Cheerful, even. 

I don't have this dark cloud following me around or anything like that. It's really just a localized stress, if that makes sense? Like, last weekend, I completely turned off my phone, literally put it in a drawer in the kitchen so I wouldn't even look at it, and my husband and I went to a local farmer's market, and I had the best time. I didn't feel down or depressed at all. I was chatting with the vendors, looking at all the fresh produce, planning out what I was going to cook for dinner that night. I ended up making this really great roasted vegetable tart, actually, which took absolutely forever to prep but was totally worth it. And the whole time, I was just happy. I wasn't feeling hopeless or empty or any of those things you just mentioned. 

It's really only when I remember that I have a commission I'm supposed to be managing that my mood tanks. But even then, it's not sadness, it's just that intense dread and anxiety I told you about. So no, I'm definitely not feeling down for most of the day. As long as I can keep my mind off the business side of things, I'm totally my normal, happy self.

Do you find yourself avoiding certain situations or interactions because you're worried about how you might come across to others—like saying the wrong thing, seeming unprofessional, or not measuring up in some way?

Well, no, not really. I mean, unless you count me staring at my computer screen for three hours avoiding sending a client an email because I'm terrified I formatted the invoice wrong, but... I think you mean in general, right? Like, just out in the world, talking to people? If that's what you mean, then definitely not. I've never really been the type to overthink my social interactions or worry if I sounded silly. 

Like, just the other day, I was at the craft store—the big one over on Route 9, because they were having a huge sale on their watercolor paper, which I always try to stock up on when it's buy-one-get-one-half-off because it gets so incredibly expensive otherwise. Anyway, I was in line, and the woman in front of me was buying all these artificial autumn flowers, and I just struck up a conversation with her about her project. We ended up chatting for like ten minutes about wreath-making, and I probably sounded completely clueless because I don't know the first thing about floral arrangements or hot glue guns, but I didn't care at all. I wasn't standing there thinking, "Oh gosh, does she think I'm stupid?" or "Did I say the wrong thing about eucalyptus?" I just like talking to people. 

And it's the exact same with our friends. Like I mentioned earlier, we have those game nights, and sometimes I'll completely misunderstand the rules of a new board game we're playing, and I'll make a totally ridiculous move that costs my team the game. My husband always teases me about it, but I just laugh it off. It doesn't make me want to hide or avoid hosting the next one. I really don't have that little voice in my head telling me I'm not measuring up or that people are judging my personality or anything like that. 

I think it's because I'm pretty comfortable with who I am, you know? I know I'm a bit of a homebody, I know I like my routines, and I'm totally fine with that. I don't feel the need to impress anyone or put on a front. It really, truly all comes back to that freelance stuff. It’s like, the second money is involved and I'm supposed to be wearing a "business owner" hat, suddenly I'm paralyzed by how I'm coming across. But just being myself, talking to people, running errands, hanging out with friends? No, I never avoid any of that. I'm an open book, really, maybe even a little too talkative sometimes, as you can probably tell! But yeah, no fear of saying the wrong thing in my normal, day-to-day life, not at all.
Do you ever feel anxious or stressed about upcoming freelance tasks or deadlines well before they actually come up, even if there's still plenty of time?

Oh, absolutely. It's like... it's like this constant, looming thing in the back of my mind. That's actually the whole reason I'm here, to be honest. I came in because ever since I tried to turn my art into a real freelance business, I just... I keep getting so incredibly wound up over things that shouldn't be a big deal, like invoices and client messages. And it starts way before anything is even due. 

Like, if someone emails me on a Monday asking about a commission, and I know I have two weeks to do it, I'll start stressing about it on Tuesday. I'll think, "Oh, I have to reply to them, I have to figure out the pricing, I have to make sure the invoice looks professional." And then I just... avoid it. I'll put it off and put it off because thinking about it makes my chest feel tight. And then, because I'm avoiding it, the stress just builds and builds until it's Friday and I haven't emailed them back, and suddenly I'm just sitting there crying at my kitchen table because I feel so overwhelmed by it all. 

And the worst part is, it starts bleeding into my actual life—the life I just told you I'm usually so good at managing! Because I'm so hyper-focused on dreading this one email or this one invoice, I'll completely blank on normal stuff. Like, last month, I was so stressed about a client asking for a revision on a piece—which, by the way, was a completely reasonable request, they just wanted the background a little lighter, but it threw me into an absolute panic—I was so stressed about it that I completely forgot to pay the electric bill. And I *never* forget to pay the bills. I have a whole system for it, a specific folder in the filing cabinet and everything. But I was just so consumed by avoiding this one art thing that the normal stuff just slipped right out of my head. So, yeah, the stress definitely starts way before the deadline, and it just kind of snowballs until I'm a mess.

Has the anxiety or dread you feel about your freelance work ever interfered with your ability to function in other important areas of your life, such as relationships, social activities, or your ability to manage household responsibilities?

Yeah, exactly, like I was just saying! It really has started affecting my home responsibilities, and honestly, the freelance work itself, too. Like, to give you a little more context on that utility payment I missed... it all happened at the exact same time I was trying to keep up with this art display I was putting together. 

There's this little independent coffee shop a few blocks from our house, and the owner is super sweet, she lets local artists hang their pieces on this big exposed brick wall they have near the espresso machines. It's a really great opportunity, but it meant I had to figure out framing and pricing tags and all this logistical stuff. And right in the middle of trying to keep up with getting that art display ready, I got that client message I mentioned. 

So instead of just taking five minutes to answer them, I completely put off the client reply because I was just so incredibly anxious about saying the wrong thing or pricing my commission wrong. And then I was so distracted by the dread of that email *and* trying to finish the display that, boom, that's exactly how the utility payment got missed. It’s like my brain just didn't have the capacity for normal life anymore. I was literally standing in my living room with a hammer and picture wire, just agonizing over this one email I was avoiding, and meanwhile, the electric bill is sitting right there on the kitchen counter in its little envelope, completely ignored. 

So, yes, it’s definitely interfering. My husband was so confused because, like I said, I'm usually the one who handles all the mail the second it comes in. I have this whole system with the filing cabinet, but all of that just went completely out the window. It's so frustrating because I want to do the art display, and I want to be responsible at home, but this whole freelance business thing just throws a massive wrench into my ability to actually get anything done.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot about making mistakes or not performing well in your freelance work, even when there's no immediate deadline or pressure?

Well, no, actually. If there isn't anything actively on my plate, like if my inbox is completely empty and I don't have any commissions lined up, I don't really think about it at all. I don't just sit around agonizing over whether I'm a good enough artist or if my technique is up to par, you know? It's really just the business side of things, the actual tasks and the expectations from other people, that gets me so worked up. 

Like, back in January, right after the holidays, things were super quiet. Nobody was asking for commissions because everyone had just spent all their money on gifts, which makes total sense, people are always tightening their budgets in January. So I had this stretch of maybe three whole weeks where I had absolutely zero freelance pressure. No deadlines, no emails to answer, no invoices to format, nothing. And I was completely fine! I felt totally normal. 

I was actually painting just for fun during that time—I did this little watercolor of a blue jay that always visits our backyard feeder, just sitting at the kitchen table in the mornings with my tea. And I wasn't worrying for a single second about whether the feathers looked professional enough, or if my shading was right, or if someone would actually pay money for it. I was just enjoying the process, exactly the way I used to before I ever tried to turn it into a business. I wasn't stressing about my performance in the slightest. 

It’s really only when that pressure is introduced—when someone reaches out and suddenly there’s an expectation, or money is involved, or a specific request needs a reply—that the panic sets in. But if there’s no pressure? If I’m just existing and there’s no immediate freelance thing hanging over my head? No, I don't worry about my performance at all. My mind just goes right back to focusing on my normal life, like figuring out what we're having for dinner, or making sure the house is tidy, or planning the next game night with our friends. So, yeah, if there's no deadline or active client, the worry just completely evaporates. It's like a light switch, honestly.
Do you find that your anxiety about freelance work has started to affect your confidence or ability to engage in social situations, even when they aren’t directly related to your job?

Oh, no, not at all. Honestly, my social life is completely untouched by this whole thing. It's really just the business side of the art that gets me. 

Like, just this past Saturday, we had our usual game night at our house. We do this thing where a couple of our friends, Sarah and Mark—Mark actually knows my husband from way back, they've known each other forever—they come over, and we usually order something or I'll cook. This time I made a huge pot of chili, the really good kind where you use a little masa flour to thicken it up at the end, and I baked cornbread from scratch in the cast iron skillet. Anyway, we were all sitting around the dining table playing this board game, Settlers of Catan, which gets incredibly competitive with our group, let me tell you. And I was totally in my element! I was loudly negotiating trades for resources, just laughing and joking around and having the absolute best time. 

I didn't feel self-conscious or anxious or anything like that. I wasn't sitting there quietly worrying about my art or feeling like I couldn't talk to them. I was just exactly how I always am—confident, chatty, completely engaged. Sarah even complimented the cornbread and I just happily chatted with her about the recipe for like twenty minutes. 

So, no, when it comes to just hanging out with people or being in social situations, I don't feel any drop in my confidence whatsoever. The anxiety is just so weirdly specific to the freelance tasks. If we go out to dinner, or if I'm chatting with the cashier at the grocery store, or talking to our neighbor Mrs. Gable when I'm out watering the hydrangeas, I'm totally fine. I don't feel shy or awkward or hesitant at all. It really doesn't bleed into my social life, thank goodness.

Do you feel anxious or extremely nervous in advance of social interactions that are related to your freelance work, like networking events, client meetings, or even pitching your art to potential buyers?

Well, no, not really. I mean, it's kind of strange, but the social, face-to-face part of it doesn't bother me at all. I don't sit in my car sweating before going into an event or anything like that. 

Like, a couple of months ago, I actually went to this local makers' meetup. It was at the library downtown—the one with the really nice new glass atrium they just built, you know? Parking is an absolute nightmare down there, especially on a Thursday evening, so I actually had my husband drop me off so I wouldn't have to deal with the parking garage. Anyway, the whole point of the meetup was to network and pitch yourself to local boutique owners and other artists. And honestly? I didn't feel nervous about going in at all. I was actually really looking forward to getting out of the house for a bit. 

I had put together this little physical portfolio binder. I had actually gone to the office supply store and spent probably way too long, like an hour, just picking out the right one because I wanted a binder that would lay completely flat when you open it, so the pages wouldn't curl up when someone was trying to look at my watercolors. So I had that all ready, and I just walked right in, grabbed a little cup of punch they had out, and walked right up to this woman who owns a gift shop over on Main Street. Her name was Diane, I think. Or maybe Deanna. 

But the point is, I just walked up and introduced myself! We talked for maybe thirty or forty minutes, just chatting about my watercolor process, how she sources local goods for her shop, what kind of foot traffic she gets in the summer, all of that. I wasn't shaking, I wasn't dreading the conversation beforehand, I didn't have any of those nervous butterflies you get when you're about to do public speaking. I just went in and talked to her like a normal person. 

It’s so weird when you think about it, because if Diane had *emailed* me and asked me to send over a formal pitch or a pricing sheet, I guarantee you I would have stared at my computer screen for three days, completely paralyzed by the thought of typing out a response and saying the wrong thing. I would have agonized over every single word. But face-to-face? Or going to a networking event? No, I don't get nervous before those at all. I actually kind of prefer it, because I can just be myself and chat, and it feels more like just making a friend than doing formal, scary business work. So yeah, the actual social interactions for the art don't make me anxious in the slightest.
Do you feel anxious or nervous in anticipation of completing a commission or delivering a piece of art to a client, even before you start working on it?

Well, actually, no. That's the funny thing about it. The actual making of the art, and even the handing it over... that part doesn't scare me before I do it. It's really just the administrative, business-y stuff that gets me tied up in knots. 

Like, if someone says they want a painting of their dog—let's say a golden retriever, because everybody loves golden retrievers, right? And they have those big, soulful eyes that are just so fun to paint. So, someone asks for a golden retriever portrait. I don't sit there dreading the actual painting part. I actually get really excited about picking out the right shades of ochre and burnt sienna, and figuring out how to capture the texture of the fur. I have this whole set of professional-grade watercolors I got for my birthday two years ago—the ones that come in those little half-pans, you know? And I love just setting up my palette and getting the paper taped down. There's no anxiety about the creation process at all.

And even the delivery part! When it's finished, and it's dried, and I've got it all packaged up nice and neat—I always put it in a clear cellophane sleeve with a piece of stiff cardboard backing so it doesn't bend in transit, and I tie a little piece of twine around it with a hand-written thank you note. It looks so professional, if I do say so myself. When I'm putting all that together, I'm just feeling proud of what I made. I don't feel nervous about handing it to them or dropping it in the mail. I'm usually just hoping they like it. 

It's really just the stuff *around* the art that makes me panic. The emails, the pricing, the contracts, the formal requests... that's where I freeze up. But the anticipation of actually doing the work or giving it to them? No, that part is completely fine. I don't feel nervous about that at all. It's just the business side that's the problem.

Do you ever feel anxious or stressed about upcoming administrative tasks related to your freelance work, like sending an invoice or responding to an email, even when there's no immediate deadline or pressure to complete them?

Oh, yes. Yes, exactly that. Honestly, that’s actually the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place. It’s just... ever since I tried to take this leap and turn my art into a real, actual freelance business, it’s like a switch flipped in my brain. I keep getting so incredibly wound up over the simplest things, like sending invoices or just checking my client messages. And it doesn't even matter if they tell me "take your time" or "no rush." The pressure is just there, constantly looming over me. 

Like, I’ll know I have an email sitting in my inbox from someone asking for a price list, and instead of just typing out a five-minute reply, I completely freeze up. I’ll avoid opening the email app entirely. I'll tell myself, "Oh, I'll do it after I wash the dishes," and then I'll find myself cleaning the entire kitchen, wiping down the baseboards, reorganizing the spice rack—doing literally anything else to avoid looking at the computer. 

And the anxiety just builds and builds in my head until I'm literally sitting there, crying at my kitchen table over a simple invoice. It’s ridiculous! I’ll be sitting there with my head in my hands, sobbing over a PDF that I just need to attach and hit send on. 

And the worst part is how it messes up the rest of my life. Because I’m spending so much mental energy avoiding these freelance tasks and getting so stressed out about them, I end up forgetting totally normal, everyday stuff. Like, last month, I completely forgot to pay our water bill. I didn't even realize it until the pink late notice came in the mail. And it's not like we didn't have the money in the checking account, I just... my brain was so overloaded and panicked about this one client message I was ignoring that I completely dropped the ball on my actual, real-life responsibilities. It’s just so frustrating to feel this paralyzed over something that's supposed to be my dream job, you know?

Do you find yourself feeling anxious or stressed about upcoming freelance administrative tasks, like sending an invoice or responding to an email, even when there's no deadline or external pressure to complete them?

Yeah, like I was just saying a second ago, that's exactly it. That's actually the whole reason I made the appointment to come see you in the first place. Because ever since I made that decision—which was supposed to be this great, empowering thing, you know?—to try and actually turn my art into a real, official freelance business, I just keep getting so incredibly wound up over those exact things. The invoices, the client messages, all the administrative stuff. 

And I just avoid them. Like I mentioned with the kitchen cleaning, I'll avoid them and put them off until I'm literally sitting there crying at my kitchen table because the pressure in my head is just too much. It's just so overwhelming, even when the client is being super nice and patient. 

And it spills over, too, which is the scary part. Because of all that avoiding and stressing over a simple email, I end up forgetting totally normal, everyday stuff. Like I said about paying the water bill! It's just... it's like my brain has no room left for basic life tasks because it's so consumed by the dread of sending a PDF. I mean, I have this beautiful little home studio set up in our spare bedroom, with all this gorgeous natural light that comes in during the afternoon, and instead of enjoying it and feeling like a real artist, I'm just hiding from my inbox, sobbing over my coffee cup, and letting the rest of my life fall apart. So, yes, definitely. That's exactly what's happening, and it's just exhausting.

Do you find yourself feeling anxious or stressed about upcoming administrative tasks related to your freelance work, like sending an invoice or responding to an email, even when those tasks are simple and straightforward?

Yes, I mean, I know I’m probably sounding like a broken record here since we just went over this, but that is exactly it. That’s the entire reason I came in to see you today. Because ever since I tried to take that step and turn my art into a real freelance business, I just keep getting so incredibly wound up over these invoices and client messages. 

And it’s exactly like you said—they are simple! They are so straightforward! It’s not like anyone is asking me to draft a massive corporate contract or negotiate some complex legal terms, it's literally just typing, "Here is the total for the watercolor portrait." But I just... I can't do it. I avoid them and avoid them, and the whole time my brain is just spinning and making it into this huge, insurmountable mountain, until I’m literally sitting there crying at my kitchen table over a two-sentence email. 

And then, like I was just saying about the water bill, it takes up so much space in my head that I end up forgetting totally normal, everyday stuff, like paying a bill on time. It’s just wild to me that something so incredibly simple and straightforward can completely derail my entire week, but that's exactly what's happening. I just get so wound up over the simplest little administrative task, and then everything else just falls apart.

Do you notice that just receiving a notification or reminder about a freelance administrative task, like an email or calendar alert, immediately triggers your anxiety, even before you actually have to do the task?

You know, it's funny you ask that, because I actually had to go in and turn off all the push notifications on my phone. I mean, every single one of them. The little red bubbles, the banners that drop down from the top of the screen, the vibrating... I had to disable all of it. Because before I did that, yes, absolutely. If my phone buzzed and I looked down and saw the little Gmail icon, or if a calendar reminder popped up saying "Follow up with Sarah about commission," my heart would just immediately drop into my stomach. 

It was like this physical reaction, you know? Just a total spike of panic, right then and there, even if I was in the middle of something completely unrelated, like folding laundry or watching a movie with my husband. Just seeing the notification would ruin my whole evening because then I couldn't stop thinking about it. I'd be sitting there on the couch, supposedly relaxing, but my mind would be racing, thinking, "Oh god, I have to reply to that, what am I going to say, what if they're mad it took me two days to answer?" 

So, yeah, I just couldn't handle the constant pings. I thought turning them off would help, and I guess it does stop that immediate jump scare of the phone buzzing, but then the problem is I still know the emails are in there, waiting for me. And then I have to actively choose to open the app, which, as I've been saying, is a whole other mountain I can't seem to climb. So I'm kind of damned if I do, damned if I don't. But to answer your question, yes, just the reminder of the task is enough to send me into a tailspin, completely. It's just exhausting living like this, constantly on edge over a little electronic ping.
Do you feel anxious or stressed just thinking about having to complete a freelance administrative task, like sending an email or invoice, even before you actually have to do it?

Yeah, I mean, that's exactly what I've been trying to say, you know? It's just the thought of it.
